prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, and its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B013 alone, to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. Having read the full first round and the chair's questions, I find that nobody disputes the physics. Kane and Mele showed that spin-orbit coupling with time-reversal symmetry gives a Z2 classification with protected edge channels. The prediction could have failed. Molenkamp's group then measured the quantised edge conduction in HgTe wells in 2007, with the right dependence on gate voltage and sample width. That is the original experiment, not a later and more elegant one, and it is exactly the theory-plus-first-observation closure I look for. Roughly eighteen years of independent confirmation by transport, photoemission and scanning probes in several material families means maturity is not an issue; B013 is the only shortlisted candidate on which no member raises a maturity objection. On the chair's distinctness question, I propose this sentence: the 2016 prize recognised topological phase transitions and Hall-type phases of matter, while this prize recognises the prediction and first measurement of a time-reversal-symmetric topological insulator, a band-structure phase with protected boundary states in a real material. I would limit the citation to the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and not claim the entire field, so that it is accurate about what these three persons did.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point and I do not want to hide it. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal for HgTe directly told Molenkamp where to look and lies outside the credited names; Zhang's death removes one possible laureate, but Bernevig and Hughes are alive and still cannot fit within three seats. Hasan's ARPES observation of the Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 surface states is an original experiment in its own right and is left out, so the three-dimensional branch goes unrecognised. Any trio of Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan leaves out someone with a serious claim, and the committee should say this openly in its internal record. A second topology prize after 2016 will also be questioned, and device applications are still scarce, though I do not think device maturity is the right yardstick for this prize.

responses.point: Eriksson would swap Mele for Hasan so that the 3D photoemission experiment is credited alongside Kane and Molenkamp, although the chair notes his own file keeps Mele.
responses.response: I have thought about this again and I still do not support the swap. Hasan's ARPES work is an original experiment and I regret leaving it out. But the primary discovery in this configuration is the quantum spin Hall state, and Kane and Mele together made the Z2 prediction (the Mele-Kane pair is the unit that appears in the record, with Kane's and Mele's two 2005 papers). Replacing Mele would credit two experiments and one half of the theory. If the committee wants the 3D branch recognised, it is a distinct achievement and should be judged as such in a later year, not squeezed into this one. I would, however, accept a citation that does not overstate the 2D story, and I would accept Eriksson's wording on first-principles closure in the internal record.

responses.point: Kroll maintains B006 for Katori and Ye as his preferred configuration, based on a clean two-name attribution, reproduction of the clocks at several institutes at the 10^-18 level, and growing use in geodesy and constant-drift limits.
responses.response: I respect that the attribution of B006 is cleaner than B013 and that independent reproduction is the correct standard for an instrument. That is why I keep it as my second alternative. My difficulty is the one I raised in round 1 and that you partly share: in the discovery sense the clock is a refinement of a precision capability that existed after 2005, and its largest impact case (the redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy) is still prospective. A first observation of a new state of matter is a different kind of statement. I note, though, that you rank B013 low only because it is outside your field and name it as your first alternative. Would you accept B013 as a single part, with B006 reconsidered once the redefinition is decided? I do not think a second part is needed.

responses.point: Mehlig wants B013 kept as a single-achievement prize and says the Kane-Mele theory is the decisive step, with Molenkamp as the first experimental realisation, while noting the trio is a defensible but incomplete story.
responses.response: I agree on a single part and on the trio. On weighting, I said in round 1 that the theory must be matched by the measurement, and I would make that a requirement in the citation: it should name both the prediction and the first observation in HgTe wells, as in the wording above. I accept your point that the idea has reached photonics, cold atoms and mechanical systems, but I would not put that in the citation, because those later realisations are not the work of the three credited persons. On B021, I take your reservation seriously, and it is mine too: the fractional charge result is secure, but the interferometric braiding evidence is too recent to be called settled.

responses.point: Danielsson moved to B013 from B008 and ends his citation on establishing topological insulators as a new class of quantum matter, while stressing that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang step goes unrecognised and wanting external reports for contested allocations.
responses.response: I used similar wording in round 1 (new class of electronic matter) but I now think it was too broad, since it edges toward the 3D branch that this trio does not cover. I therefore end the citation on the first observation in HgTe quantum wells. Your point on commissioning outside reports is right and I support it: an external check of priority between the BHZ proposal and the Kane-Mele and Molenkamp work, and of Hasan's priority for the 3D case, should be obtained before the vote. I also remain with you on B008: I cannot support a one-name prize for a collaboration discovery.

responses.point: Lindroth prefers B002 for Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, built on the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and quantum gas microscopes, and acknowledges that five credited names are squeezed into three seats and that she may be biased by being closest to atomic physics.
responses.response: I find the Mott-insulator observation and the quantum gas microscope to be real experimental milestones, and your frank statement of the attribution problem is the kind of care I want. Our difference is that for B002 the original-experiment question has no unique answer: the Bose-Hubbard proposal (Jaksch and Zoller) and the 2002 experiment (Greiner, Bloch and Hänsch) involve names outside your trio, and Esslinger's Fermi gas work is a parallel line. For B013 the priority record is much sharper. Since you list B013 as your first alternative, would you accept it as a single part?

uncertainties: Whether the committee can accept the omission of Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang authors in internal record and citation wording, or whether an outside priority report would change the allocation.

Whether the one-sentence distinction from the 2016 prize (band-structure topology protected by time-reversal symmetry in real materials, as opposed to topological phase transitions and Hall-type phases) will convince the members who raised it.
For the alternatives, whether Andrei's earlier STM flat-band observation in B025 should displace one of the credited trio, and whether the pairing mechanism will be settled soon.
My recollection of exact priority dates (the 2005 Kane-Mele papers, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang in 2006, Molenkamp in 2007) is from memory and not checked against the primary papers.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for B013. I have no known collaboration with Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or Hasan. I am a Chalmers colleague of Johansson, who has stated his connection to B009; B009 is not part of my configuration, so this does not bear on my vote. I also work in the electron microscopy and materials-characterisation community, but I know of no tie to Andrei (B025) or to the clock or cold-atom candidates. I repeat that I make my judgement on the priority record and not on field loyalty or on counts of support.
